steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid)

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks one oxygen atom at the 2' carbon).  
   • RNA: Ribose (has a hydroxyl –OH group at the 2' carbon).  
   → The extra –OH in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G).  
   • RNA: Adenine (A), Uracil (U) replaces thymine, Cytosine (C), Guanine (G).

3. Strandedness and shape  
   • DNA: Usually double-stranded, forming a long antiparallel double helix.  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded and can fold into diverse 3-D shapes (hairpins, loops, etc.); some viruses have double-stranded RNA genomes.

4. Length and overall size  
   • DNA: Very long (millions to billions of nucleotides), encoding whole genomes.  
   • RNA: Typically shorter—range from <100 nt (e.g., tRNA) to several thousand nt (e.g., mRNA). Exceptions are RNA viral genomes.

5. Cellular location  
   • DNA: Confined to nucleus in eukaryotes (and in mitochondria/chloroplasts); nucleoid in prokaryotes.  
   • RNA: Synthesized in nucleus but functions mainly in cytoplasm; found in many cellular compartments (ribosomes, nucleolus, mitochondria, etc.).

6. Stability  
   • DNA: Highly stable; good for long-term genetic storage.  
   • RNA: More prone to hydrolysis; suited for short-term tasks like information transfer, catalysis, regulation.

7. Functions  
   • DNA: Long-term storage of genetic information, template for replication, transcription.  
   • RNA: Multiple roles  
     – mRNA: conveys genetic code from DNA to ribosome  
     – rRNA: structural/catalytic component of ribosomes  
     – tRNA: brings amino acids during protein synthesis  
     – Regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, etc.)  
     – Catalytic RNAs (ribozymes)  
     – Genomic material for some viruses.

8. Replication and synthesis  
   • DNA is replicated by DNA polymerases during cell division.  
   • RNA is transcribed from DNA by RNA polymerases; some RNA viruses replicate RNA directly.

9. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA has extensive repair systems (mismatch repair, excision repair, etc.).  
   • RNA generally lacks repair; damaged RNAs are degraded and replaced.

Summary  
DNA is a long-term, double-stranded, thymine-containing, deoxyribose-based molecule optimized for stable genetic storage. RNA is a usually single-stranded, uracil-containing, ribose-based molecule whose extra hydroxyl group confers flexibility and catalytic potential, enabling it to act as messenger, adaptor, ribozyme, regulator, and, in some viruses, as the genetic material itself.
